title: Which bands were really innovative: Bobby Sherwood and George Barnes
summary: Schremp names Kenton, Herman and Raeburn as the three adventurous bands; Handy dismisses Sherwood's claim.

story.theme_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section: instruments and players
story.community_name: Banjo, guitar and the rhythm section's changing role

blocks.x: Let's go back to that recording session. The reason it's important-- let's go back beyond that and talk about some things.

This is, I guess, more Boyd than George, there were two or three really innovative bands then, that is, people cutting across the grain and doing what the hell they wanted to do; one with Stan and Woody and this band. There were others who kind of touched on the edges of civilization, but those were the three, I think; am I missing somebody who was really cutting across the grain?
No, that was about it. There are a lot of guys who since have claimed that they were innovative at the same time; that is a bunch of bullshit.
I don't know who would be.
One for instance claimed that he was one of the first, or he was the first innovative writers to appear on the scene was this guy, Bobby Sherwood; remember him?
Yeah. His music was interesting and a little bit off balance sometime, but surely nothing musically extraordinary.

I never thought there was anything interesting or innovative about his stuff, and he pointed to a thing that he had written called "March of the something--" He had written this thing which was one of his big sellers; he got a good play on the thing.
I can't give you the title of that; I know what you're talking about.
I heard the thing and I didn't find a thing innovative about it, but he seemed to feel that that was the first new approach that had been done.
That's not to be taken seriously.
There were people in those days, George Barnes--not George Barnes--yeah, George Barnes, the guitar player--
He was doing interesting and kind of different things, not of this order or magnitude.

He was doing--it may have been a little bit later--George was the house band, if you can believe, at the Pump Room in Chicago, the Ambassador East. He had been a quintet, a guitar, a piano and maybe harp, bassoon and oboe; I just make that up, I really don't remember, but it was that kind of thing, and he was doing Ray Scott kind of things, something obviously he had listened to you, and I probably should say he was doing inventive, original material, though I can't remember the book that well. He had some claim to--at least trying to swing something.
